power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Cognitive theories are among the leading conceptualizations of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
The core perspective shared by these theories is that distorted thinking (e.g., "no one can be trusted") is involved in maintaining symptoms.

However, the proximal mechanisms linking cognition and PTSD symptoms remains unclear due to two major methodological limitations: 1) lack of research on cognition-symptom dynamics at the daily level, and 2) reliance on self-reported thought distortions, which is a method ill-suited for capturing biases that people often do not have insight into or are outside of their awareness.
The present study helps address these limitations in a sample of trauma-exposed patients (N=510) who completed daily video diaries and symptom ratings for 90 days (n=30,958 days).
We used two natural language processing techniques to assess cognitive distortions from the diary transcripts: a lexica-based and large language model (LLM) approach.
We then established the day-to-day sequencing of cognitive distortion and symptom fluctuations using dynamic structural equation models.
Across the lexical and LLM models, distorted thinking did not predict worsening symptoms (s=-.02-.01).
Instead, worsening symptoms predicted more distorted thinking (s=.03-.07).
Also, symptoms and cognitive distortions tended to fluctuate together (s=.08-.41).
The current findings suggest that cognitive distortions do not precede PTSD symptoms as many theories have assumed, but may instead be a consequence or correlate of them.
If replicated, our results could help refine cognitive and related models of PTSD.
Cognitive theories are a leading conceptualization of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
The core hypothesis shared by these models is that distorted thinking provokes and maintains symptoms over time.
Cognitive distortions include biases such as catastrophizing (e.g., "if I go back there, I'll completely lose control") or overgeneralizing (e.g., "the world is fundamentally unsafe").
Although the specifics vary across theories, distortion-symptom mechanisms can be distilled into three basic temporal patterns.

The most widely recognized of these is the hypothesis that cognition is a proximal precipitant of PTSD symptoms (i.e., cognitive vulnerability). [1] [2] [3] [4] That is, when people engage in maladaptive cognitive processes, these thoughts lead to symptoms like avoidance, hyperarousal, dysphoria, or re-experiencing.

text.text: This hypothesized sequence of thoughts to symptoms is the reason cognitions are a primary target in many frontline PTSD treatments. [5] [6] [7] [8] Two other temporal patterns connecting cognitive distortions to PTSD symptoms are possible but have received less attention.

text.text: A second mechanism is the reverse of cognitive vulnerability, such that symptoms lead to cognitive distortions (i.e., cognitive reactivity). 9, 10 Cognitive reactivity could reflect various processes including mood-congruent attentional and interpretive biases 11 or maladaptive appraisals about symptoms themselves (e.g., "my intrusions are a sign of going crazy"). 12, 13 Finally, a third mechanism may be that symptoms and cognitive distortions are elicited by same situations (i.e., cognition-symptom coactivation) rather than one driving the other. 14, 15 The mechanisms underlying these three temporal patterns are not necessarily mutually exclusive, and are intertwined with other behavioral responses, but they nonetheless form the foundation of cognitive theories. 14, 15

text.text: Cross-sectional research consistently shows that people diagnosed with PTSD and those with more severe symptoms endorse more distorted thinking (e.g., catastrophizing, personalization). 12, 16, 17 Longitudinal studies suggest that the severity of distorted thinking before or shortly after trauma exposure predicts the likelihood of developing PTSD weeks or months later. [18] [19] [20] [21] Results from treatment studies are more mixed, with results showing changes in cognitive distortions precede symptom changes (but not vice versa), changes in distortions both predict and follow changes in symptoms, cognition and symptoms change concurrently, and that cognitive changes do not predict symptom changes at all. 5, 6, [22] [23] [24] [25] Thus, the bulk of evidence suggests that distorted thinking relates to PTSD, but the relative strength of each mechanism is unclear or whether cognitive vulnerability is, in fact, as prominent as theories would suggest.

text.text: Methodological limitations have hindered a more definitive test of mechanisms proposed by cognitive theories. 26 Two are especially relevant: First, all longitudinal studies to date have included only a small number of time points (i.e., < 4) separated by weeks or months rather than ambulatory assessment or daily diary designs, which increases the influence of recall bias and misses short-term dynamics between thoughts and symptoms. 27, 28 Indeed, processes at a short time scale are considered especially important to understand according to cognitive theories, which posit that thoughts triggered by everyday reminders of the trauma event and its sequelae elicit symptoms and prolong PTSD. 2, 15 The only study that examined such short-term dynamics with an ambulatory assessment design found re-experiencing symptoms and cognitive distortions tracked together within a day, consistent with coactivation mechanisms. 29 However, because this study focused only on concurrent associations, the temporal order of cognitive distortions and symptoms at short time scales remains unknown.

text.text: The second limitation to date is that cognitive distortions in PTSD have only been measured with self-report surveys.
One problem with this method is that the survey items are often very similar or even identical to PTSD symptom criteria.

Most obviously, criterion D2 in the DSM for PTSD is "persistent exaggerated negative beliefs about oneself, the world, and others," 30 which is essentially the same as cognitive distortion survey items like "the world is a dangerous place" or "there is something wrong with me as a person." 13 Such overlapping content can blur the distinction between predictor and outcome, limiting our ability to infer mechanistic relationships.

text.text: Another more fundamental problem is that self-report questionnaires are simply an ill-suited method for the construct because cognitive distortions are, by definition, automatic and often occur outside of conscious awareness. 31 Moreover, people often lack insight into their biases, [32] [33] [34] especially when they become ingrained beliefs as is often the case in PTSD. 4, 35, 36 A method that overcomes these problems with self-report measures is to assess cognitive distortions directly from the language people use when describing their unique experiences, with natural language processing. 37 In particular, people's responses to open-ended prompts may reveal subtle or implicit thinking patterns that they may have limited awareness of 38, 39 and would be missed by a self-report distortions measure.

text.text: This feature makes analyzing cognitive distortions from language a uniquely strong fit to the construct. 40 Further, because it is an entirely distinct method from a questionnaire, it is unconfounded with reported symptoms.

text.text: Two modeling approaches can be applied to measure cognitive distortions from natural language: 41 1) Lexical models that count the frequency of certain words or short phrases associated with thought distortions, and 2) zero-shot estimation with large language models (LLMs), which involves prompting an LLM to assess cognitive distortions from text without task-specific training. 42, 43 Reinforcing the value of this method for testing cognitive theory, cross-sectional work has shown language-based measures of cognitive distortions have strong associations with internalizing psychopathology (e.g., depression). [44] [45] [46] Despite this potential, language-based assessments of cognitive distortions have not yet been used to understand PTSD maintenance mechanisms.

text.text: A strong test of cognitive theories could benefit from tracking cognitive distortions measured from language and symptom dynamics at a short time scale that matches the hypothesized processes.

This study capitalized on a unique dataset to address limits of prior work and rigorously test the three basic mechanisms proposed by cognitive theories: cognitive vulnerability, cognitive reactivity, and cognition-symptom coactivation.
We studied a sample of trauma-exposed patients with elevated PTSD symptoms who completed daily video diaries and symptom ratings for 90 days.
From these diaries, we measured daily cognitive distortions using two natural language processing approaches: a lexical model and zero-shot prompting of an LLM.
Using dynamic structural equation models, we established the temporal order of cognitive distortions detected from language and day-to-day symptom fluctuations.
These models allowed us to compare the strength of these mechanisms head-to-head, at the daily level, for the first time.
This was secondary analysis of data from a project aiming to develop tools for automated monitoring of PTSD symptom severity.
Study procedures were approved by the Stony Brook University institutional review board.
Data was collected between 2022 and 2025.
Participants were recruited from two sources.
Majority (71%) were World Trade Center disaster responders recruited from the Stony Brook World Trade Center Health Program.
Remaining participants were trauma-exposed outpatients from the Stony Brook University Hospital system.
To be eligible, participants had to have elevated PTSD symptoms (PTSD checklist for the DSM-5 [PCL] 47 scores > 12).

Due to the study protocol's complexity, individuals with cognitive impairment were ineligible (Montreal Cognitive Assessment 48 (MoCA) score < 18).

text.text: Participation involved an in-person laboratory session followed by a 90-day daily diary protocol.

During the initial session, participants were consented and trained on the daily diary protocol, which consisted of recording a video diary on their personal smart device and completing a brief self-report survey of PTSD symptom severity each day.
Participants received $5 per post (i.e., survey and video).
Analyses included 510 participants, with a total of 30,958 days (average days per person = 80.0, SD = 18.5).

text.text: Daily PTSD symptoms.

PTSD symptom severity was assessed using 8 items adapted from the PCL-5. 47 This scale has been validated for use in ambulatory assessment settings and did not include cognitive symptoms. 49 Participants rated symptom severity on a scale from 1 ("not at all") to 5 ("extremely").

text.text: Total PTSD symptom severity was calculated by averaging all items.
Cognitive distortions were assessed from language in the daily video diaries.

For these recordings, participants were trained to discuss emotionally relevant topics related to their day. 50 They could select their own topics or follow example prompts (e.g., "tell me about the worst part of your day," "describe when you felt most happy today").

text.text: Recordings were required to be 3-10 minutes long.
Audio from the videos was transcribed using Whisper 51 and cognitive distortions were scored from the resulting text.

We assessed cognitive distortions with two modeling approaches: lexical and zero-shot models.

Lexical models were developed to detect words and phrases indexing 12 cognitive distortions related to depression. 52 Word spans were selected to be common expressions that capture the core of each distortion type.

text.text: Zero-shot models involved scoring cognitive distortions using an LLM without taskspecific training (i.e., using just what was learned from the base training data).

Specifically, we prompted GPT-5.1 (2025-12-31) to rate the overall prominence of 12 cognitive distortions (same types scored by the lexical models) in each diary text from 0 (not at all present) to 10 (present in most of the transcript).

We used established lexical models for positive and negative tone 38, 57 as well as affective valence and arousal. 58

text.text: Our analyses used dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM), 59 conducted in Mplus (Version 8.11). 60 DSEM combines multilevel models with time series analysis to estimate within-person temporal dynamics.
text.formatted: Our analyses used dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM), <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59</ref> conducted in Mplus (Version 8.11). <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">60</ref> DSEM combines multilevel models with time series analysis to estimate within-person temporal dynamics.

text.text: With DSEM, each daily variable (i.e., cognitive distortions and PTSD symptoms) is decomposed into between-person and within-person latent variables.

Between-person variables reflect each person's average level of cognitive distortions and symptoms, whereas within-person variables capture fluctuations in distorted thinking and symptoms from their average levels on a given day.
At the within-person level, we estimated temporal paths representing cognitive vulnerability, cognitive reactivity, and cognition-symptom coactivation.
Model set-up is shown in Figure 1.
text.formatted: Model set-up is shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Paths were modeled as random effects, which allows the strength of dynamics to vary across people.
Cognitive vulnerability is the lagged association between cognitive distortions and changes in next-day symptoms.
Cognitive reactivity is the lagged association between symptoms and changes in next-day cognitive distortions.
Finally, cognition-symptom coactivation is the correlation between changes in cognitive distortions and symptoms on the same day.
To ensure the lagged effects capture predicted change in next-day symptoms or cognitive distortions, autoregressive paths were estimated as random effects.
At the betweenperson level, random intercepts for cognitive distortions and symptoms were correlated, which is akin to a cross-sectional association between distorted thinking and symptom severity.
Separate models were estimated for lexical and zero-shot distortion scores.
DSEMs assume there are equal intervals between measurement occasions, but this was not always the case in our sample due to occasional missing days of data (due to e.g., incomplete surveys).

We accommodated for this by coding missing days and modeling the missingness with full information techniques. 59 DSEM uses Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), meaning point estimates are drawn from the posterior distribution of values generated for that parameter.

text.text: Because there are no p-values with this approach, parameters are tested based on whether zero is within their 95% credibility interval (CrI).
There was substantial within-person variability in cognitive distortions and symptoms.

Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) indicated that there is more within-person (versus between-person) variance in distortions (ICClexical = .27; ICCzero-shot = .41), whereas there is slightly more between-person variance in symptoms (ICC = .61).
In other words, these results suggest cognitive distortions are more situation-dependent, while PTSD symptoms are more trait-like.
Figure 2 depicts the dynamic interplay of distortions and symptoms for three randomly selected participants.

text.text: These plots show both how much these variables fluctuate from day-to-day and that those fluctuations appear to track with one another.
Given the novelty of this application of language-based cognitive distortions, we also evaluated their validity in several ways.
First, we compared the language-based scores to human ratings.
Seven trained research assistants rated the overall presence of cognitive distortions in a subset of 165 transcripts.
Interrater reliability was adequate, with a two-way mixed absolute ICC of .62.
Human ratings were strongly correlated with both the lexical (r = .31; 95% CrI [.17, .44]) and zero-shot scores (r = .68; 95% CrI [.60, .78]), further supporting their validity.
Second, we examined convergent validity between the two language-based methods.
There was clear evidence of convergence at both the between (r = .56; 95% CrI [.50, .63]) and within-person levels (r = .20; 95% CrI [.18, .20]), indicating they measure similar constructs.
Third, we replicated well-established cross-sectional associations between cognitive distortions and PTSD symptoms.

At the between-person level, overall severity of distortions and symptoms were strongly correlated, for both language models (rlexical = .32; 95% CrI [.23, .40]; rzero-shot = .61; 95% CrI [.55, .67]).
Finally, we more closely evaluated the content validity of zero-shot scores because this method has not been applied to cognitive distortions before.
Specifically, we examined GPT's rationale for ratings.
Rationales were obtained during the scoring procedure by requesting GPT provide a brief explanation justifying the score, citing specific phrases from the transcript (full prompt in Table S1).

In particular, the rationales for low scores suggest an ability to differentiate general distress or superficial signs of distorted thinking from "true" distortions.

text.text: The lexical and zero-shot DSEM results were highly consistent with each other.
Results for the within-person level testing the three mechanisms are in Figure 1.

text.text: Contrary to the cognitive vulnerability hypothesis, cognitive distortions did not predict next-day symptoms in either model.
Instead, results were consistent with cognitive reactivity, such that worsening symptoms predict more next-day cognitive distortions (βlexical=.03; βzero-shot=.07).
There was also support for cognition-symptom coactivation, with the strongest associations being between same-day cognitive distortions and symptoms (βlexical=.08; βzero-shot=.41).

Although not of focal interest to our study, it is worth noting that the autoregressive paths (shown in Figure 1) suggest there is less day-to-day "spill-over" in cognitive distortions (βlexical=.06; βzero-shot=.13) compared to symptoms (β=.30).

text.text: We conducted two sets of sensitivity analyses.
First, we tested the specificity of our results.
It is possible that the effects of cognitive distortion variables on symptoms were driven by expressions of negative emotions rather than distorted thinking per se.

We tested this possibility with DSEMs estimating the unique associations between distortions and symptoms over and above language-based measures of positive and negative tone as well as emotional valence and arousal.
In these models, distortions and an emotion variable were included as simultaneous predictors of same-day symptoms at the within-person level, and of overall symptoms at the between-person level.
No lagged paths were included for a maximally conservative test focusing on the strongest associations in our main analyses (i.e., within-and between-person covariance).
Results were unambiguous; cognitive distortions (both lexical and zero-shot) predicted symptoms over and above emotion language, at both within-and betweenperson levels.
Moreover, the magnitude of association with symptoms changed very little after adjusting for emotional language (average  decrease within-person = .01; between-person = .05).
Full results are in Table S3-S4.

text.text: These findings reinforce that our main results speak to the unique role of cognitive distortions--not just emotions--in PTSD symptom maintenance.
Second, we tested the generalizability of results across populations.
For these analyses, we estimated the main DSEMs separately for WTC responders versus the general traumaexposed outpatients.

text.text: This study provided an unprecedented test of cognitive theories in PTSD.

In a head-to-head comparison of candidate mechanisms, at a timescale matching the hypothesized processes, and with cognitive distortion measures that can detect automatic, implicit thinking patterns, we find no evidence that distorted thoughts precipitate symptoms.
Instead, our results suggest that cognitive distortions are the consequence or correlate of symptoms.

If replicated, these findings can help articulate a more precise model for understanding and treating PTSD. 1 The only exception was that the 95% CrI for lexical cognitive reactivity included zero in the general outpatient sample.
text.formatted: If replicated, these findings can help articulate a more precise model for understanding and treating PTSD. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> The only exception was that the 95% CrI for lexical cognitive reactivity included zero in the general outpatient sample.

text.text: However, this discrepancy is likely due to reduced precision of the relatively small sample size (n = 146 vs. 364), and we consider the effect to have been replicated because the point estimate fell within the CrI for cognitive reactivity in the WTC responder sample.
Our principal finding is that a central hypothesis of many cognitive theories--that thoughts lead to symptoms--is not supported once key methodological limitations are addressed.

While surprising, these results do help make sense of the mixed evidence for cognitive vulnerability in the literature to date. [63] [64] [65] The only real consistent finding has been that there is some association between PTSD and cognitive distortions when measured cross-sectionally or at weekly and monthly intervals. 12, [16] [17] [18] [19] [20] [21] Indeed, we replicated these results in our study, finding strong correlations between symptoms and distortions at the between-person level.

text.text: Yet, when we zoomed into day-to-day symptom-distortion dynamics, we were able to clarify which short-term mechanisms are likely driving these cross-sectional and long-term associations found in prior work.
The strongest dynamic found was symptom-cognition coactivation.

Previous ambulatory assessment studies of self-report cognitive distortions and depression suggested coactivation and cognitive vulnerability may be at play. [66] [67] [68] However, implications for cognitive theories were unclear because overlapping scale content and shared rater biases muddied the distinction between constructs.

text.text: By assessing cognitive distortions in natural language, there was less opportunity for a methodological confound with symptom expression.

Not only are the language-based measures an entirely different method from a self-report survey, but we showed they are not simply picking up on emotional language, reinforcing the distinctiveness from symptoms.
All told, this method allowed for more conclusive evidence that distortions track with trauma-related distress, while not predicting future symptoms.

This could indicate cognitive distortions are a symptom of PTSD, which would align with the DSM-5 definition that includes negative cognitions as a criterion. 30 Alternatively, this could imply cognitive distortions are merely an epiphenomenon of symptoms.

text.text: Although our results alone cannot adjudicate these interpretations, they provide a solid empirical foundation to inform ongoing efforts to define the core pathology of PTSD.
According to our results, cognitive reactivity may be a key mechanism underpinning PTSD.
This account for the role of distortions has been primarily studied in relation to depression, 10, 63, 69, 70 and here we find it may extend to trauma-related symptoms.

text.text: There are several explanations for why symptoms would lead to cognitive distortions rather than the other way around.

One possibility is that distress activates mood-congruent attentional and interpretive biases. 11 Another possibility is that many traumatized people have persistent, negatively biased cognitions, but these thoughts are usually corrected through effortful processing.
text.formatted: One possibility is that distress activates mood-congruent attentional and interpretive biases. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> Another possibility is that many traumatized people have persistent, negatively biased cognitions, but these thoughts are usually corrected through effortful processing.

text.text: When symptoms worsen though, regulating distress may deplete cognitive resources needed to correct thinking biases, leading to increases in cognitive distortions. 64 Yet another possibility is that symptoms trigger distorted thoughts directly, as people often have maladaptive appraisals of symptoms (e.g., "I should be able to handle my reactions better"). 71, 72 Investigating these explanations for cognitive reactivity in PTSD will be a productive direction for future research.

text.text: Our study presents an unprecedented test of mechanisms proposed by cognitive theories of PTSD.
If the findings replicate, our theories must be updated.

Namely, cognitive theories must be able to account for the observed coactivation and cognitive reactivity effects, and the primary role of cognitive vulnerability revised to reflect the absence of evidence for it.
Another consideration for theory development our study underscores are that the time scale of cognitionsymptom processes is underspecified in current models.
This issue limits the models' utility because it renders the core claims about mechanisms difficult to falsify.
For example, we examined the daily timescale because processes are described as reactions to everyday events, but perhaps cognitions trigger symptoms on the order of seconds, minutes, or hours.

Whether cognitive vulnerability (or any other mechanism) unfolds day-to-day versus minute-to-minute not only has vastly different conceptual implications, but it also dictates the appropriate study design. 73, 74 Specifying the timescale of processes will make cognitive theories more precise, testable, and ultimately useful for understanding PTSD.

text.text: Research wise, a top priority is to evaluate whether our results replicate.
Another natural next step is to determine whether the findings generalize beyond PTSD.

Cognitive theory is widely accepted as a generic framework that explains most psychopathology. 65, 75, 76 According to a generic cognitive model, various psychological dysfunctions result from distorted thinking, but disorders are distinguished by specific situational triggers and thought content. 75 For example, social anxiety would relate to self-conscious thought content whereas health anxiety relates to health-related content.

text.text: Assessing distortions from open-ended narratives enable a true test of the generic cognitive model by separately analyzing thought content from biased processing.

Models in our study assessed distorted thought processes, and core content domains (e.g., self-consciousness, health) could be assessed with zero-shot or another language-based method like topic modeling. 77 With these methods, it becomes feasible to test whether a) all psychopathology symptoms are driven by cognitive processes and b) thought content differentiates disorders.

text.text: Our results may also have significant clinical implications.

Frontline psychotherapies for PTSD--and many other psychiatric disorders--include interventions designed to reduce symptoms by changing thoughts. [78] [79] [80] If our results replicate and cognitions are actually a consequence or correlate rather than cause of symptoms, then this could help explain the limited efficacy of our frontline cognitive treatments. [81] [82] [83] Importantly, another implication is that we could potentially improve PTSD treatment by targeting cognitive reactivity (with e.g., mindfulness-based therapies) instead. 84, 85

text.text: Limitations of our study should be considered.
One limitation is that results may not generalize to all trauma-exposed populations.
Although our sample we showed results were robust across two distinct populations (WTC responders and general outpatients), participants were disproportionately White and male.
Analyses should be replicated in samples with greater racial and gender diversity to ensure generalizability of results.
Another limitation is that we cannot directly compare our results to prior work because we did not have self-report cognitive distortion measures.
Of course, our motivation for using language-based measures was to address shortcomings of self-reported cognition, so the lack of self-reports is also a strength.
Nevertheless, studies with both types of distortion measures administered in the same sample would allow for more direct connections to existing literature.
Despite being the dominant paradigm in PTSD theory and treatment, there have been gaps in knowledge about the maintenance mechanisms proposed by cognitive models.
Our study begins to address this gap by applying novel methodologies uniquely suited to test the central hypotheses of cognitive theories.
If replicated, our results call for a revision of cognitive theories in PTSD and suggest a path forward for redesigning treatment to be more effective.
